cards.title: Sample complexity of uniformity testing with less than one stored sample
cards.formal: Determine the minimum sample count q*(n,ε,m) for one-pass uniformity testing with m bits of persistent memory, including when this count is infinite, in the scarce-memory regime m=o(max{log₂ n,log₂(1/ε)}). Here n≥2 is an integer, 0<ε<1, and m≥1 is an integer. The tester receives independent samples from an unknown distribution P on [n], must accept P=Uₙ with probability at least 3/4, and must reject every P with ‖P−Uₙ‖₁≥ε with probability at least 3/4. The central case in the source is fixed ε and m=o(log n); the displayed wider regime is its explicit extension for small ε. Determine matching asymptotic upper and lower bounds up to universal constant factors in sample count throughout the stated regime.
cards.why: Would locate the statistical power of streaming computation below the memory needed to retain one observation and determine whether extra samples can compensate for this severe storage restriction.
cards.status_note: Checked the complete 2019, 2021 and 2022 papers, including the later paper’s explicit distinction between time-varying and time-invariant updates. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution of the stated time-varying scarce-memory sample tradeoff; this is not an exhaustive current-status certification.

cards.definitions: Write [n]={1,…,n}, Uₙ(j)=1/n, and ‖P−Uₙ‖₁=Σⱼ₌₁ⁿ|P(j)−1/n|. A tester with horizon q is a layered randomized streaming machine: after t samples its state M_t lies in a set of at most 2^m possibilities. An initial state or initial state distribution is fixed independently of P. At step t its new state is chosen using only M_{t−1}, the current sample X_t and fresh independent randomness. The transition kernel may depend on t,n,ε,m,q, but not on P. After exactly q samples it outputs a Boolean decision from M_q, possibly with fresh randomness. Every item of retained information, including retained random bits, belongs to the state; past samples cannot be revisited. The current input symbol is available for the transition without first being copied into persistent memory. Transition tables, the layer index and computation between arrivals are not charged as extra memory; no uniform construction-time or running-time bound is imposed. This is the time-varying information-theoretic streaming convention, not a single fixed transition rule forced to store its own clock. Probability is over the independent sample stream and all tester randomness. q* is the least nonnegative integer q admitting such a tester, and is ∞ if no finite q works. The source’s little-o regime means parameter sequences with n→∞ and m/max{log₂ n,log₂(1/ε)}→0; constants in the requested sample bounds do not depend on those parameters. No correctness promise is imposed at intermediate distances 0<‖P−Uₙ‖₁<ε.
cards.answer_criterion: Characterize exactly which parameter sequences in the stated scarce-memory regime permit finite-sample testing and give a sample bound with a matching lower bound up to constant factors there. Lower bounds must apply to all of the defined time-varying randomized streaming testers, not only collision-based algorithms or time-invariant machines.

context_blocks.title: Memory can be smaller than one alphabet symbol
context_blocks.text: Recording a single sample from an n-element domain takes about log₂ n bits. The question asks what testing remains possible when the tester cannot retain even one complete observation, and how much additional data can compensate for that restriction.

context_blocks.title: A distribution property rather than full estimation
context_blocks.text: The tester only distinguishes the uniform law from laws separated by a fixed ℓ₁ gap. It need not reconstruct individual probabilities, and its decision must work for every alternative distribution satisfying the promise.

context_blocks.title: Known collision bounds do not cover the unresolved regime
context_blocks.text: The 2021 construction processes batches of stored samples. Its discussion after Corollary 10 explicitly leaves scarce memory open. The printed bound must not be extrapolated below the memory needed for those stored samples merely by substituting a small m into its formula.

context_blocks.title: A later lower bound uses a different clock convention
context_blocks.text: Berg, Ordentlich and Shayevitz prove logarithmic-in-n memory lower bounds for fixed distance in a model with a time-invariant transition rule and asymptotic time-averaged error. They explicitly distinguish the earlier, more permissive time-varying streaming model. Their theorem therefore does not settle the finite-horizon question stated here.

cards.context:
Recording a single sample from an n-element domain takes about log₂ n bits. The question asks what testing remains possible when the tester cannot retain even one complete observation, and how much additional data can compensate for that restriction.

The tester only distinguishes the uniform law from laws separated by a fixed ℓ₁ gap. It need not reconstruct individual probabilities, and its decision must work for every alternative distribution satisfying the promise.

The 2021 construction processes batches of stored samples. Its discussion after Corollary 10 explicitly leaves scarce memory open. The printed bound must not be extrapolated below the memory needed for those stored samples merely by substituting a small m into its formula.

Berg, Ordentlich and Shayevitz prove logarithmic-in-n memory lower bounds for fixed distance in a model with a time-invariant transition rule and asymptotic time-averaged error. They explicitly distinguish the earlier, more permissive time-varying streaming model. Their theorem therefore does not settle the finite-horizon question stated here.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
